rss_0_1786648036.title: DRC’s fast-growing Ebola outbreak spreads to sixth province
rss_0_1786648036.text:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has spread to a sixth province, officials have said, a day after the head of the World Health Organization said the outbreak was on track to surpass the deadliest in history, which killed at least 11,000 people more than a decade ago.

The current outbreak has killed more than 2,100 people out of more than 4,500 cases, according to the latest government figures released on Tuesday. At the same point in the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, the previous most deadly outbreak, 755 cases had been recorded, according to WHO data.

Jean Kaseya, the director general of Africa CDC, said on Thursday that a death had been recorded in the previously unaffected Bas-Uele province. The man had travelled from Isiro, in Haut-Uele province, to Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele, where he died, Kaseya said.

There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current outbreak.

The death toll has been reached almost three times faster than in the 2014-16 outbreak. On Wednesday, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said the current outbreak would surpass that one based on its current pace.

Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have now been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported.

Uganda has reported 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case there was reported on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded.

The DRC outbreak is unfolding amid strikes by some unpaid health workers, global development aid cuts, threats by rebel groups, anger from long-traumatised communities, and misinformation claiming that Ebola is not real.

Health workers at the Nizi treatment centre in Ituri province went on strike on Thursday, leading to the temporary closure of the centre, saying they had not been paid for three months.

The true scope of the outbreak remains unknown. It was declared on 15 May but the WHO says sequencing now shows it began months earlier in February.

Health authorities have said between 60% and 70% of new cases are recorded outside contacts being monitored, and that the disease is spreading at an alarming rate.

Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, the WHO regional director for Africa, said this week: “We are chasing the virus; the virus is ahead of us.”

Nonetheless, his colleague Abdirahman Mahamud, the head of the WHO’s emergency response division, sounded a note of optimism on Wednesday, saying that if the pandemic response was implemented “at the same time across the five transmission zones, we are expecting a turnaround in three months”.

Even with that, Mahamud said the peak of the outbreak would not be reached for six months under a “moderate” scenario and that the outbreak could last nine to 12 months.

Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from body fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, including from dead bodies, and from contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.

Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola causing this outbreak began last month in Ituri. Tedros said on Wednesday two vaccines developed specifically for this strain were now being tested on people for the first time.

This strain of Bundibugyo is genetically different from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012, making it likely that this outbreak began when the virus jumped from an infected animal to a human, researchers said in a paper published this week in the journal Nature Medicine. They had sequenced genomes from samples from 22 people with Ebola.

Last week, Kaseya said officials were worried the virus could be mutating and that the Africa CDC was planning further studies with the WHO to investigate.

Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this story.

rss_1_1786648036.title: French ambassador to CAR investigated over claims he hosted dozens of women
rss_1_1786648036.text:
France has opened disciplinary proceedings against its ambassador to Central African Republic over allegations of misconduct, after claims he brought dozens of women into his official residence, raising potential security concerns.

The investigation comes as Paris seeks to rebuild relations with CAR after their sharp deterioration in recent years amid Russia’s expanding influence in the former French colony.

The French weekly newspaper Le Canard enchaîné reported that the ambassador, Bruno Foucher, 65, brought about 30 women between the ages of 20 and 30 into his residence during the period of January 2024 to March 2026, with some of them staying overnight. The visits prompted officials to report a security breach.

The ambassador acknowledged having had sexual relations with two young women, the weekly said.

The French foreign ministry said: “At the initiative of the ministry, an administrative investigation was carried out in Bangui in 2026. Upon receipt of the findings of this mission, and at the request of the minister, the ministry initiated disciplinary proceedings against the ambassador. These proceedings are ongoing.”

The ministry conducted an on-site inspection in April, which led to the opening of disciplinary proceedings.

Foucher is a career diplomat who has served as ambassador to CAR since 2023. He was ambassador to Lebanon from 2017 to 2020, to Iran from 2011 to 2016, and to Chad between 2006 and 2011.

According to Le Canard enchaîné, which said it obtained the inspection report, the ambassador received about 15 visits a month.

He also allegedly instructed staff to allow one of the young women to stay at the residence during his absence.

Russia maintains a strong foothold in CAR, primarily through the Wagner paramilitary group, which plays a key role in providing security for the country’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra.

French officials have accused Russians of fostering anti-French sentiment in a number of African countries.

The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, praised the “complete restoration of relations” between France and CAR when he visited Bangui in March.

rss_2_1786648036.title: Zambia elections haunted by ghost of incumbent president’s arch-rival
rss_2_1786648036.text:
As Zambians go to the polls on Thursday, the ghost of the current president’s predecessor hangs over the elections.

Hakainde Hichilema, 64, is bidding for a second term leading the southern African country after defeating his arch-rival Edgar Lungu by a landslide in 2021.

A feud between the two men, their families and supporters has dominated Zambian politics, to the extent that the quarrel has continued even after Lungu died in South Africa in June 2025.

Zambia’s government went to court to try to stop the burial of Lungu by his family, who did not want Hichilema presiding over a state funeral. In June, South Africa’s supreme court of appeal ruled in favour of Lungu’s family, overturning a previous high court decision in favour of the government.

View image in fullscreen Edgar Lungu and his wife at a rally in Lusaka in 2015. Photograph: Rogan Ward/Reuters

In this election, Hichilema is facing the Tonse Alliance of opposition parties led by Brian Mundubile, 55, who was a government chief whip under Lungu. Mundubile’s running mate Makebi Zulu acted as the Lungu family’s spokesperson during the burial row, and on the campaign trail the two men have promised to bring Lungu’s body back to Zambia for a dignified burial.

The way death is dealt with is very important in Zambia, said Christopher Vandome, a senior research fellow at the thinktank Chatham House. “Even Hichilema supporters want to see due respect given to those that have died,” he said. “When it appears things get messy, it just makes the incumbent look disrespectful.”

The shadow of Lungu has also hung over allegations by the Tonse Alliance that Hichilema has deployed authoritarian tactics during the election campaign, including raiding its offices and detaining 36 members of Mundubile’s team.

Hichilema’s team furiously denied the claims, invoking Lungu’s treatment of Hichilema during the last election. “Zambians know what repression looks like. In 2021, the opposition leader [Hichilema] had been arrested 15 times, Prime TV [a private station] and the Post [a newspaper] had been shut down, and on election day the internet was switched off,” said a spokesperson for the ruling United Party for National Development. “Today the opposition campaigns freely across all 10 provinces, no media house has been closed and the airwaves are open.”

View image in fullscreen Brian Mundubile, the main opposition challenger, waves to supporters as he leaves a radio station in Lusaka. Photograph: Gianluigi Guercia/AFP/Getty

Transparency International Zambia monitors have recorded incidents of police interrupting opposition rallies, said Tamika Halwiindi, a coordinator at the organisation. “Disruptions from the police citing issues to do with safety have been noted to be more biased against the opposition and independents, as opposed to … the ruling party,” she said.

During Hichilema’s term, activists have also reported having peaceful demonstrations shut down. Mputa Ngalande of the Fight Inequality Alliance said he was among a group detained for more than 12 hours in July 2024 when they were protesting against the state power company during a period of 22-hour-a-day blackouts.

Vandome said: “[Hichilema’s] prospects of winning are very high. But his … personal lived experience of how complicated Zambian elections can be has given him this insecurity which is actually counting against him … denting his image in a way he doesn’t have to.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to The Long Wave Nesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the world Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Zambia’s economy has stabilised since an economic crisis, which was triggered when it defaulted on its debts in 2020 under Lungu. Annual inflation is now 6.5%, compared with 24.6% in July 2021. The government made primary and secondary education free in 2022.

View image in fullscreen Supporters of Hakainde Hichilema and the United Party for National Development gather at a campaign rally in Lusaka. Photograph: Gianluigi Guercia/AFP/Getty

Meanwhile, Zambia has attracted more international investment in recent years due to its huge deposits of copper, a key material in green technologies.

At the start of the month, in a giveaway to young voters, Hichilema, also known by his initials HH and nickname Bally (a slang word for an elder), told a crowd of jubilant university students that he was increasing their accommodation allowance by 50% with immediate effect.

However, the cost of living could still count against Hichilema in the elections, in which almost 8.8 million registered voters will also choose MPs and local councillors. The average annual income rose from $1,127 to $1,318 between 2021 and 2025, according to World Bank data. But prices almost doubled over the same period.

“What people are asking is: ‘If we are doing well economically, why are we not feeling impact on the ground?’” said Ngalende. “Because you will find on the ground that it is very difficult to access three meals a day.”

rss_3_1786648036.title: At least 44 dead after overcrowded ferry capsizes on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe
rss_3_1786648036.text:
At least 44 people have died after an overcrowded ferry capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe, police said.

The boat had a capacity of 90 people, but was carrying 114 adult passengers, five crew members and an unknown number of children, Zimbabwe’s civil protection unit (CPU) said earlier on Wednesday, citing ticket sales.

A crew member told the national broadcaster ZBC that there were 153 people onboard when the ferry overturned on Tuesday after it hit large waves. A passenger told ZBC that the boat began taking on water about 30 minutes after it left the lakeshore town of Kariba, heading for islands and fishing camps.

A specialised underwater team was flown to the area, the CPU said, as search and rescue continued on Wednesday. At the time, the CPU said the death toll was 15, with 27 known to be missing.

Zimbabwe’s police updated the death toll on Wednesday afternoon in posts on X twice in the space of 32 minutes. In the first post, it said the death toll was 38, adding: “The bodies have been retrieved from the lake.” Then it said that 44 people were now known to have died.

A video shared by ZBC on Tuesday showed several people appearing to be sitting on the upturned ferry, while at least four speedboats came to their aid and a helicopter circled overhead.

Maxwell Kanhema Page, who describes himself as a media practitioner and originally posted the video shared by ZBC, reshared a video on his Facebook page filmed from the shore, in which he had noted that the lake was “angry”.

He said: “A few moments later I get over 200 calls about [the ferry] sinking. A sad day indeed.”

Lake Kariba is the world’s largest human-made lake by volume, stretching about 150 miles along Zimbabwe’s northern border with Zambia. It was created in the 1950s during British colonial rule, when the Zambezi River was dammed, displacing about 57,000 people. The Kariba dam supplies at least a third of both countries’ electricity.

It is not uncommon for boats to overturn on the lake. In 2014, 26 people, 24 of them children, drowned in Zambia’s part of the lake, when the boat meant to transport them to independence day celebrations capsized.

On the Zimbabwean side, five drowned in a 2021 incident and three were feared dead in an October 2023 capsizing. The month before, a police boat overturned although no one died.

Agence France-Presse contributed to this report.

rss_4_1786648036.title: Halting the march of the African armyworm: a natural cure offers hope to farmers
rss_4_1786648036.text:
Hearing about fields full of dead caterpillars enveloped in a mysterious white substance intrigued the South African scientist Letodi Luki Mathulwe. Something was killing off the African armyworm – one of the most devastating pests for farmers in east and southern Africa.

The white substance was a naturally occurring fungus and it was wiping out the caterpillar, which gained its name from its march-like advance through fields of crops.

An outbreak of African armyworm (Spodoptera exempta) in 2025 had started in northern South Africa and by April had reached the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal, where Mathulwe was working for the agriculture department. Every day she was getting panicked calls from local farmers who were finding the caterpillars in their fields.

Mathulwe went out to the KwaZulu-Natal countryside to see for herself and it was there, in the fields of Kikuyu grass – crucial grazing for livestock – that she realised she had made an important discovery.

View image in fullscreen Armyworms eating grass. A soil fungus could offer a new way to tackle the hugely destructive caterpillars where chemical controls have fallen short. Photograph: Letodi Luki Mathulwe

“Something was killing the insects naturally. I was intrigued because in other areas the insects were alive and destroying the grass but as soon as they come here, there’s something that is killing them,” she said.

As an entomologist who had studied the use of fungi to kill insect pests, Mathulwe immediately gathered samples of the dead armyworms and the fungus to test at her laboratory in Pietermaritzburg.

Her team’s results, now presented in a peer-reviewed research paper, showed she was right in her hunch that the fungus could be used in the fight against the armyworms.

It was a major breakthrough, said Mathulwe, because while there are chemical treatments for dealing with the caterpillars in the early stages of life, nothing has proven effective against mature populations.

The African armyworm not only eats staple crops such as maize and sorghum but also releases a chemical compound in grass that can make cattle sick.

The impact can be brutal for farmers. One outbreak in 2017 was estimated to have destroyed up to 40% of Zambia’s maize production.

View image in fullscreen Major outbreaks of armyworms have threatened the food security of some African countries. Photograph: Courtesy of Letodi Luki Mathulwe

It also sends food prices soaring and puts strain on government budgets. Last year’s outbreak caused problems for farmers in countries such as Zimbabwe, where inflation had hit 736% in 2024, and Malawi, where it reached 35% in 2024.

The African armyworm causes the most damage in its caterpillar stage but is also hard to control when it develops into a moth, allowing populations to migrate.

“When we discovered this fungus, we realised we could develop this into a product that can be eventually used when the next outbreak happens,” said Mathulwe.

“I think it will be a great thing – it will eventually eliminate the fear for farmers that the insect creates because once it’s present within grazing fields, farmers start to panic.”

Mathulwe said there was still more work and more testing to do in developing a product for use by farmers.

“I think it will create a lot of hope for farmers, because it will mean that their animals won’t get sick if the farmer is able to control the presence of the insects within their field,” she said.

rss_5_1786648036.title: Former Mexican governor charged in case of 43 students who vanished in 2014
rss_5_1786648036.text:
The former governor of Guerrero state in Mexico has been formally charged over his alleged involvement in the disappearance of 43 students in 2014, a case that has become a symbol of the country’s brutal cartel violence and government impunity.

Ángel Aguirre, who was arrested last week, is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice for ordering the destruction of surveillance tapes that may have shed light on what happened to the students from the Ayotzinapa teacher training college on the night of 26 September 2014.

On Wednesday, a judge ruled Mexico’s attorney general had presented enough evidence to formally charge Aguirre with forced disappearance and ordered that he remain in a maximum security prison awaiting trial.

A lawyer for Aguirre denied his client’s wrongdoing. Guillermo Baradas told reporters: “We presented evidence demonstrating a high-level meeting attended by Mr Ángel Aguirre at the time the videos were allegedly handed over to him.”

Aguirre’s indictment is the biggest breakthrough in the Ayotzinapa case since the 2022 arrest of Jesús Murillo Karam, who served as Mexico’s attorney general at the time of the students’ abduction.

The brutality of the case rocked Mexico and continues to haunt the country more than a decade on. With the remains of only three students identified, it is not known what happened to the 40 others.

On the night that they were abducted, the students from the Raúl Isidros Burgos teacher training college in the village of Ayotzinapa had commandeered several buses in the city of Iguala to get to a protest in Mexico City.

But before they could leave Iguala, in Guerrero state, the students were attacked by a local criminal gang working with municipal police. A years-long international investigation determined that federal forces, both police and military, were also involved either by participating directly or failing to intervene as the students were taken away and presumably killed.

The government at the time orchestrated an elaborate coverup, attempting to place blame for the attack solely on the criminal gang and local police. Suspects were tortured into giving false confessions and crime scene evidence was manipulated.

Meltión Ortega, a spokesperson for the 43 students, said: “We want no more deception; we want to be told the truth and for those responsible to be punished. The victims from Guerrero deserve to have the actual perpetrators and the masterminds punished, rather than just seeing a charade, as has happened in serious cases of human rights violations.”

Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has vowed to get to the bottom of what happened to the students and formed an investigative unit to dig into the case last year. “I’m going to put all my effort, all my energy, all my willpower [towards obtaining truth and justice],” she told reporters at a news conference last week.

rss_6_1786648036.title: Canadian airline WestJet agrees to settle flight attendants’ sexual harassment class action
rss_6_1786648036.text:
The Canadian airline WestJet has agreed to pay C$4.5m (£2.4m) to settle a decade-long sexual harassment class action lawsuit levelled by its female flight attendants, who alleged the company failed to maintain a safe workplace.

The suit followed allegations by Mandalena Lewis, a former flight attendant, that a pilot had sexually assaulted her and a colleague, but that WestJet kept the pilot flying, thereby putting other employees at risk.

A British Columbia judge on Monday approved the terms of the settlement, which were finalised on 22 June after months of negotiation. The payment will be distributed among the 3,452 flight attendants in the class action after expenses are removed, including legal fees.

WestJet agreed to hire a third-party to conduct a workplace inquiry that will examine the prevalence of harassment, the extent of underreporting and how reporting systems can be made more effective.

The suit had called on WestJet to implement mandatory anti-harassment training for pilots, along with an admission of wrongdoing and an admission of a breach of employee contract. None were included in the settlement.

Lewis filed the initial class action against the airline in April 2016. She said she was dismayed by the results, especially given that two years ago WestJet paid out $12.5m in a baggage fee class action, nearly three times the amount agreed to in the sexual harassment suit.

“I’m glad it’s over … but I’m just exhausted. I’m shaking my head,” she said, adding that she was advised the amount was the most that could be achieved given that legal expenses were piling up.

Under BC law, the suit included all female flight attendants who worked for the company between 4 April 2014 and 28 February 2021, because Lewis’s suit alleged that all of them had their contracts violated by WestJet during that period because its employee policy promised that the workplace would be free from harassment.

The suit claimed WestJet broke its policy by not taking enough steps to address reports of assault or to prevent harassment in the first place.

Lewis said she was sexually assaulted by a WestJet pilot while on a layover in Hawaii in 2010 when she was 25 years old. In court documents, she said the same pilot had also assaulted another flight attendant in 2008.

Though she reported the assault to WestJet, the pilot remained at the company and Lewis was eventually fired in 2016 for “gross insubordination”, according to court documents submitted by WestJet that year, which she and her legal team allege was retaliation for trying to hold the airline accountable internally.

She said she abandoned an individual civil claim and instead created the class action after learning other flight attendants had also experienced harassment.

Lewis said she reported the assault to police in Maui but alleges WestJet rerouted the pilot so he would not face questioning in Hawaii.

She said fellow members of the class action suit were also disappointed with the result. Eight of them had already asked the province’s supreme court not to approve the settlement in February when some of the details first emerged, citing a low payout and a lack of accountability by WestJet.

“We didn’t get justice here,” said Lewis.

The case garnered national attention for exposing pilot behaviour toward female flight attendants and the vulnerability of the scores of young women who have historically been the target demographic for the job.

A 2018 survey of more than 3,500 flight attendants by the US Association of Flight Attendants found that 68% had experienced sexual harassment in their careers while only 7% had reported an incident to their employer.

WestJet did not respond to questions about Lewis’s claims of assault, and the allegations that it failed to keep the workplace free of harassment and does not properly investigate alleged sexual assaults.

In a statement, the company said it was “pleased to have reached a mutually agreed upon settlement”. It said: “We are committed to strengthening our operations and training, focused on the safety and wellbeing of all WestJetters and we are focused on advancing a culture of empowerment.”

rss_7_1786648037.title: Canadian airline cancels flight after child refuses to wear seatbelt
rss_7_1786648037.text:
A Canadian airline cancelled a flight from Victoria to Toronto after a child refused to wear a seatbelt.

The child was standing in their chair as the 6 August Porter Airlines flight taxied towards the runway, the airline said. Repeated attempts by an accompanying parent and crew to secure the child in their seat failed, so the crew elected to return to the terminal and have the two passengers disembark as “the aircraft could not take off in this unsafe condition”, it added.

Brad Cicero, a spokesperson for the airline, told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) that all passengers had to disembark, as the time needed to remove only the child and their parent and refile paperwork meant the plane could not take off before the airport closed at 12:30am.

“We apologise for the effect this had on other passengers, who were able to depart on a flight the following day,” he told the broadcaster.

Passenger Aryeh Kozuch told the Canadian Press that the child was not being unruly, and that online comments admonishing the parents did not “empathetically capture the situation”.

“They just kept hiding under their seat,” he said. “If they got forced into [being] strapped in, they just kind of slid out underneath.”

“This was a child that was in a tube with 150 people … They’re obviously terrified, and their response was to try and hide under the seat in front of them,” he said. “That’s so different than a kid running around and screaming.”

Hillary Hertzberg, another passenger, said the airline could have acted faster. “It took for ever,” Hertzberg told CBC. “The kid eventually got off the plane at 11.30 so we had been on the flight for almost an hour at that point.”

Porter Airlines said passengers were rebooked on a different flight the following day.

rss_8_1786648037.title: Scores dead in Colombia after powerful earthquake strikes west of country
rss_8_1786648037.text:
More than 100 people died after a powerful earthquake struck western Colombia, collapsing and severely damaging scores of buildings in major cities including Cali and Pereira.

The US and Colombian geological surveys reported that a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck at 7.34am local time on Monday, with its epicentre in the western department of Chocó. It was felt in neighbouring Venezuela, still reeling from a deadly double earthquake on 24 June.

The quake killed at least 132 people and more than 570 were injured as of Monday afternoon, according to the Colombian Association of Capital Cities, a group coordinating cities across the country.

View image in fullscreen Rescue workers raise their fists to call for silence as they attempt to find people under the rubble of a collapsed building in Cali. Photograph: Sergio Acero/Reuters

“The ⁠national government has all of its capabilities deployed to protect lives, assist affected communities and deliver aid wherever it is ​needed,” Colombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said in a national address at about 1pm local time upon declaring ‌a national state of emergency. “The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble.”

Western Colombia appeared to have suffered the most serious damage. Authorities reported 27 deaths in the Valle del Cauca department, 40 deaths in Pereira, the capital of Risaralda department, and at least two in Manizales, the capital of Caldas.

The mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas Giraldo, said at least 12 buildings and 20 homes had been partially or completely or destroyed.

In a video post, he told citizens to be “completely ready” for aftershocks. “Do not go back into the buildings yet. I know this isn’t easy but stay outside for a little while at least because there could be an aftershock.”

Social media videos showed people searching for victims in the wreckage of a four-storey hotel in Cali and a woman sprinting from a building as it collapsed in Manizales.

One video showed part of San José church in Pereira collapsing as palm trees around it shook. Another video published by the newspaper El Tiempo captured the moment a building gave way in Manizales.

View image in fullscreen Local people and rescue workers search for people under a collapsed building in Cali’s La Alameda neighbourhood. Photograph: Samir Rojas/Getty Images

The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said at least 20 buildings collapsed in his city and people were trapped inside.

“Right now, we are trying to map out what has happened, firstly to protect lives and secondly to be able to push ahead with any kind of rescue that might be necessary,” he said, urging citizens to stay calm.

He told residents to check their buildings for structural damage. “If you do not feel safe, if you see very large cracks, please leave the building.”

In an interview, the mayor of Pereira, Mauricio Salazar, said 65 buildings had collapsed, with victims thought to be trapped in at least 15 of them. Five of the city’s hospitals were reportedly inundated with the injured.

Buildings damaged after strong earthquake hits Colombia

Raúl Andrés Buitrago, the head of customer service at a business in Pereira, said he was leaving for work when the seismic alert on his watch went off.

“There are often little tremors here,” he said. “But I’d never felt an earthquake like this. It started softly, softly, softly, then it felt like it was getting stronger every second.”

He spoke of “horrible” scenes as he fled outside on to the street in the city centre, which is home to many old buildings. “The roofs started to fall in. The buildings collapsed in on themselves. The panic was terrible. They were the four longest minutes of my life.”

View image in fullscreen Rescuers work in Cali in the early hours of Tuesday morning. Photograph: Sergio Acero/Reuters

The governor of Chocó, Nubia Carolina Córdoba, said people had been injured and buildings severely damaged in the department’s capital, Quibdó.

De la Espriella, who took office on Friday, said he would lead the government response. “Colombia has a president whose heart aches for his people and who will do everything in his power to help them in the most difficult moments,” he said in a video post.

View image in fullscreen A woman carries her cat after an evacuation in Bogotá. Photograph: Raúl Arboleda/AFP/Getty Images

De La Espriella visited Quibdo where he promised rent subsidies for those who had lost homes, and then travelled to Cali. Authorities ‌in Cali, Armenia and Manizales announced curfews, with Cali’s mayor saying threats of looting had forced him to deploy police and military personnel to the streets. De La Espriella promised 1,000 additional security personnel for the city.

Aviation authorities said the airports were damaged in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Cartago, Armenia and Buenaventura.

View image in fullscreen The cathedral of Manizales was damaged in the earthquake. Photograph: John Jairo Bonilla/AP

Neighbouring Venezuela was struck on 24 June by twin earthquakes that devastated the country’s northern coast, killing more than 6,000 people.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the Trump administration – which has thrown its weight behind Colombia’s new rightwing president – would provide $15.5m in emergency aid.

rss_9_1786648037.title: Colombia quake leaves more than 110 dead – as it happened
rss_9_1786648037.text:
3d ago 01.04 EDT Closing summary We’re about to wrap up this live coverage of Colombia’s devastating earthquake but you can read an updated full report here – and below is a recap of the day’s news. It’s now a little after midnight local time. Search and rescue efforts were under way early on Tuesday in dozens of cities and towns in western Colombia after a powerful earthquake struck the region.

At least 110 people were killed after the 7.4-magnitude quake struck on Monday morning local time, toppling buildings, damaging hospitals and infrastructure and trapping people beneath the rubble in Colombia’s strongest earthquake this century.

More than 2,700 people had been reported missing by Monday night.

New president Abelardo de la Espriella – sworn in just days earlier – declared a state of emergency and said in an address to the nation that his government had deployed all of its capabilities “to protect lives, assist affected ‌communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed”.

“The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble,” de la Espriella said after about 1,600 buildings had been damaged , including at least 61 that completely collapsed.

Colombian volunteers and rescuers were sifting through rubble into Monday evening searching for survivors. A person among those who joined a make-shift crew in Cali – western Colombia’s largest city – said: “We are trying to get everyone out alive.” View image in fullscreen Volunteers help remove debris at a collapsed building in Pereira, western Colombia. Photograph: Gabriel Aponte/Getty Images Local officials confirmed deaths across several regions, including the coffee region of Risaralda. Among the worst-hit areas was the city of Pereira, with at least 40 deaths reported; the department of Chocó, with at least 12; and the neighbouring Valle del Cauca department with at least 27, including 15 in Cali, Colombia’s third most populous city.

The quake hit the remote Chocó region about 7.30am local time and was felt as far as Bogotá, the national capital, about 400km (250 miles) away, as well as in neighbouring countries Ecuador, Venezuela and Panama. The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people, and the initial quake was followed by two aftershocks of 2.8 and 4.8 magnitude.

Authorities ‌in the cities of Cali, Armenia and Manizales announced curfews in the aftermath of the quake , with Cali’s mayor saying threats of looting had forced him to deploy police and military personnel to the streets.

The US state department announced it would provide $15.5m for emergency shelter, food and other aid. Governments across Latin America also offered help.

The earthquake comes less than two months after back-to-back quakes devastated parts of Venezuela, killing more than 6,100 people. Share Updated at 01.32 EDT

3d ago 00.19 EDT Amid the quake devastation in western Colombia, little is known about the extent of the damage in Chocó, a remote region where officials reported dozens of injured people and damaged buildings but few other details. Phone signals were out in many parts of the region’s capital, Quibdo. The town closest to the earthquake’s epicentre, San Jose del Palmar, has no airport and is located on top of a mountain ridge along a highway linking the cities of Cali and Pereira.
